stem: A client with heart failure has been advised to reduce dietary sodium. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of practical sodium-reduction strategies?

options.A: I will compare Nutrition Facts labels, choose lower-sodium packaged foods, and use herbs, spices, citrus, or vinegar instead of adding salt for flavor.
options.B: I can rely on taste to identify high-sodium foods, so reading labels is unnecessary if a food does not taste salty.
options.C: Processed and restaurant foods contribute little sodium, so I should focus mainly on removing the saltshaker from the table.
options.D: I should increase table salt at meals because sodium restriction is not relevant to dietary management when heart failure is present.

rationale: Current American Heart Association nutrition guidance recommends comparing Nutrition Facts labels and choosing products with less sodium; it also recommends using herbs, spices, citrus, and other flavorings in place of added salt. AHA notes that most dietary sodium comes from packaged, prepared, and restaurant foods, so taste alone or removing only the saltshaker is not sufficient. Therefore, A demonstrates correct understanding. B and C underestimate hidden sodium, and D reverses the advised dietary strategy.
educational_objective: Apply practical sodium-reduction strategies by reading labels, choosing lower-sodium prepared foods, and replacing added salt with non-sodium flavorings.
source_document_title: How to Reduce Sodium in Your Diet; AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations
source_version_date: AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations last reviewed 2026-03-31; sodium guidance current 2026
source_locator: How to Reduce Sodium in Your Diet → shopping: compare packaged/prepared-food labels and select lower-sodium products; preparation: use onions, garlic, herbs, spices, citrus juices, and vinegars instead of salt. AHA Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations → choose whole/minimally processed foods, foods low in sodium/prepared with little or no salt, and read Nutrition Facts/ingredient labels. Sodium Sources guidance: more than 70% of U.S. dietary sodium comes from packaged or restaurant foods.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports label reading, lower-sodium food selection, limiting sodium from packaged/prepared foods, and using herbs/spices/citrus/vinegar instead of salt without imposing a heart-failure-specific universal sodium target.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort → Nutrition and Oral Hydration: evaluate nutritional status and implement special diets/dietary modifications based on diagnosis and client needs; provide nutrition-related client education.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — dietary sodium modification for a client with heart failure
correction_summary: Reclassified the item from Safety/Infection Prevention and Control to Basic Care and Comfort and narrowed the construct to practical sodium-reduction behaviors. The final item avoids a universal heart-failure sodium number because the HF guideline notes uncertainty regarding optimal restriction thresholds; it tests directly supported label-reading and food-preparation strategies instead.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Dietary sodium-reduction education in heart failure
audit_findings.source_authority: Current official American Heart Association nutrition guidance; no secondary nutrition source used.
audit_findings.currentness: AHA's overall diet/lifestyle recommendations were reviewed March 31, 2026 and the sodium-reduction resources remain current at the audit date.

claim_by_claim.stem: The client has already been advised to reduce sodium, avoiding a claim that every HF client requires an identical sodium prescription.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because all listed strategies are directly recommended by current AHA nutrition guidance.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because sodium may be present in foods that do not taste obviously salty and label comparison is recommended.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because most sodium in the U.S. diet comes from packaged, prepared, and restaurant foods, not solely table salt.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because it contradicts the prescribed dietary-reduction plan and current low-sodium heart-healthy guidance.
claim_by_claim.rationale: No universal milligram target or claim that sodium restriction independently improves HF mortality/hospitalization is introduced.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests taste-based estimation, C saltshaker-only thinking, and D reverses the intervention. Each reflects a plausible nutrition misconception.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A consists entirely of evidence-supported sodium-reduction behaviors.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are client statements about sodium management and have similar declarative form.
audit_findings.blueprint: Basic Care and Comfort is the strongest fit because the item tests dietary modification and nutrition education for an existing illness.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited for an unsupported heart-failure sodium threshold and for whether processed foods should be categorically avoided. The final wording says choose lower-sodium packaged foods rather than banning all processed foods and omits a universal numeric limit. No unresolved conflict remains.
